title: Quectel 5G — Alternative (InfluxQL + live)
description: Live radio snapshot read from the router plus signal history from InfluxDB. Every panel carries an explanation behind the small "i" in its top-left corner -- hover it if a number or an acronym is unfamiliar. In short: RSRP is how strong the signal is, SINR is how clean it is and is the one that predicts speed, and the number of carriers is how much spectrum is in use. Generated by quectel-5g-tools/grafana/generate_alternative.py.

panels.title: Network
panels.description:
The mobile network the modem is registered with. Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape.

Reads *no service* when the modem is not registered at all -- searching, out of coverage, or no usable SIM.

panels.title: Mode
panels.description:
How 5G is attached. `NSA` (non-standalone) is 5G carried on top of an LTE anchor and is the usual case; `SA` is standalone 5G with no LTE underneath.

A dash means there is no 5G leg at all and the modem is on LTE alone -- the same condition the NR panels show as *no NR*.

panels.title: RRC
panels.description:
The radio connection state the modem reports: `CONNECT` while a link is actively carrying data, `NOCONN` when it is camped on a cell with nothing to send, `SEARCH` while looking for one, `LIMSRV` for limited service (emergency calls only).

`NOCONN` is **not** a fault. An idle link sits there most of the time; it says nothing about signal quality.

panels.title: NR RSRP
panels.description:
**RSRP** is raw signal strength, in dBm: how much of the tower's signal reaches the antenna. It is always negative and closer to zero is stronger -- green from -80, red below -100.

This is the 5G carrier. Reads *no NR* whenever the 5G leg is detached and the modem is running on LTE alone.

Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape.

panels.title: NR SINR
panels.description:
**SINR** is signal *quality*, in dB: how far the wanted signal stands above noise and interference. This is the one that predicts speed -- green from 20, red below 0, where the link struggles however healthy RSRP looks.

This is the 5G carrier, and it is the value to aim a directional antenna by -- the one `5g-monitor` turns into beeps so you can point without watching a screen.

Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape.

panels.title: LTE RSRP
panels.description:
**RSRP** is raw signal strength, in dBm: how much of the tower's signal reaches the antenna. It is always negative and closer to zero is stronger -- green from -80, red below -100.

This is the 4G carrier. In NSA mode it is also the anchor the 5G leg is bolted to, so it is worth watching even when 5G is doing the work: lose the anchor and the 5G goes with it.

Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape.

panels.title: LTE SINR
panels.description:
**SINR** is signal *quality*, in dB: how far the wanted signal stands above noise and interference. This is the one that predicts speed -- green from 20, red below 0, where the link struggles however healthy RSRP looks.

This is the 4G carrier.

Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape.

panels.title: Connected carriers
panels.description:
Every carrier the modem is using at once. Mobile networks bond several channels together (carrier aggregation) to go faster, so **more rows here generally means more throughput** -- this is often what explains a speed change the signal numbers do not.

- **Role** -- `pcc` is the primary carrier, `scc` a secondary added on top.
- **Band** -- the block of spectrum. Low bands (LTE 20, 5G n28) travel far and pass through obstacles; high ones (LTE 7, n78) are much faster but shorter-ranged.
- **PCI** -- identifies which cell of that band, out of 504 possible codes. A change of PCI is a change of cell.
- **MHz / BW** -- centre frequency and channel width. Wider is faster.

Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape.

panels.title: Neighbour cells
panels.description:
Other cells the modem can hear but is **not** using, strongest first. These are the candidates it would hand over to, so the list is a measure of how much company you have: a healthy list means somewhere to go if the serving cell fades, and a list thinning towards empty is the first sign of running out of coverage.

- **Scope** -- `intra` is a neighbour on the same frequency as the serving cell, `inter` one on a different frequency.
- **ARFCN** -- the channel number the cell transmits on.
- **PCI** -- identifies the cell within that channel.

Read live from the router each time the dashboard refreshes, and stored nowhere -- this is *now*, not the last scrape. The history of this list is summarised by *Neighbours reported* below; the rows themselves are never kept.

panels.title: RSRP
panels.description:
**RSRP** is raw signal strength, in dBm: how much of the tower's signal reaches the antenna. It is always negative and closer to zero is stronger -- green from -80, red below -100.

One line per band, so a handover onto different spectrum shows as one line stopping and another starting rather than as a jump in a single line. Gaps are polls where nothing was reported, drawn as a break rather than as a zero -- a reading nobody took is not a reading of zero.

targets.query: SELECT mean("rsrp") FROM "quectel_nr5g" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "band" fill(none)
SELECT mean("rsrp") FROM "quectel_lte" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "band" fill(none)

panels.title: SINR
panels.description:
**SINR** is signal *quality*, in dB: how far the wanted signal stands above noise and interference. This is the one that predicts speed -- green from 20, red below 0, where the link struggles however healthy RSRP looks.

Worth reading against RSRP to its left: **strength holding steady while quality falls is interference, not a pointing problem**, and no amount of turning the antenna will fix it. Both falling together is a coverage or aim problem. Gaps are polls where nothing was reported, drawn as a break rather than as a zero -- a reading nobody took is not a reading of zero.

targets.query: SELECT mean("sinr") FROM "quectel_nr5g" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "band" fill(none)
SELECT mean("sinr") FROM "quectel_lte" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "band" fill(none)

panels.title: RSRQ
panels.description:
**RSRQ** is quality in dB adjusted for how busy the cell is. It sags when the tower is congested while RSRP holds steady, so a fall here with no fall in strength usually means other users rather than worse aim. Green from -10, red below -15.

Gaps are polls where nothing was reported, drawn as a break rather than as a zero -- a reading nobody took is not a reading of zero.

targets.query: SELECT mean("rsrq") FROM "quectel_nr5g" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval) fill(none)
SELECT mean("rsrq") FROM "quectel_lte" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval) fill(none)

panels.title: Carriers in use
panels.description:
Which carriers were actually in use over time, as blocks rather than lines. Each row is one carrier and its colour is that carrier's RSRP on the usual scale, so a row that turns red was still in use but weak.

**Row labels read "role technology band".** `pcc lte 3` is the primary carrier on LTE band 3; `scc 5g 78` a secondary on 5G n78. Role is part of the label because intra-band aggregation is ordinary -- two carriers can sit on the same band at once, and without the role there would be nothing to tell them apart.

**The number inside each block is that carrier's RSRP in dBm** -- signal strength, always negative, closer to zero is stronger, green from -80 and red below -100 like everywhere else here. It is not a count, a band number or an id. The unit is left off so that narrow blocks stay readable, and Grafana drops the number altogether when a block is too narrow to fit it; the colour carries the same reading either way.

**A row that stops is a carrier that was dropped; a row that starts is one that was added.** That is the quickest read of a handover or of the 5G leg detaching.

Rows are every carrier seen anywhere in the selected time range, not the ones up right now, so widening the range adds rows for carriers long since left behind. *Connected carriers* at the top of the dashboard is where "right now" lives.

targets.query: SELECT last("rsrp") FROM "quectel_carrier_pcc", "quectel_carrier_scc" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "role", "rat", "band" fill(none)

panels.title: Serving site (eNodeB)
panels.description:
Which LTE base station is serving the modem, as its numeric identity (the eNodeB id, shared by all cells on one mast).

**The value on the axis means nothing as a quantity -- read the steps, not the height.** Each step is a handover to a different site. A flat line is a link sitting still on one mast; frequent steps mean the vessel is moving between them, and a step that coincides with a dip in RSRP above is a handover you felt.

targets.query: SELECT last("enodeb") FROM "quectel_lte" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval) fill(previous)

panels.title: Neighbours reported
panels.description:
How many neighbouring cells the modem could hear at each poll, split into `intra` (same frequency as the serving cell) and `inter` (a different one). The cells themselves are listed in *Neighbour cells* at the top of the dashboard.

**A thinning count is an early warning of running out of coverage, and it usually moves before RSRP does** -- you lose the alternatives before you lose the cell you are on.

Gaps are polls that returned no sample, drawn as a break rather than as zero: no neighbours reported and no reading taken are different things.

Kept for 24 hours only -- neighbour lists churn constantly on a moving vessel, so they live in a short-retention bucket of their own. Ranges longer than a day will look empty here.

targets.query: SELECT count("rsrp") FROM "quectel_neighbour" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "scope" fill(none)

panels.title: Aggregated carriers
panels.description:
How many carriers were bonded together at each poll, split by technology. This is the count behind the *Connected carriers* table at the top.

More carriers means more spectrum in use and, broadly, more speed, so **a drop here often explains a slowdown that the signal panels do not** -- the network can withdraw a carrier under load while every dB stays exactly where it was.

targets.query: SELECT count("rsrp") FROM "quectel_carrier_pcc", "quectel_carrier_scc" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "rat" fill(none)

panels.title: Carrier frequency
panels.description:
The centre frequency of each carrier in use. Shown as megahertz rather than as a band number because the useful question at sea is usually *did it fall back to low band*, and that is easier to see on an axis than to remember band by band.

Roughly: **below 1000 MHz** travels a long way and passes through obstacles but is slow; **1800-2600 MHz** is the middle ground; **3400-3800 MHz** (n78) is the fastest and the shortest-ranged. A line dropping to the bottom of the chart is the modem trading speed for reach, which is usually the right call and always worth knowing about.

targets.query: SELECT mean("frequency_mhz") FROM "quectel_carrier_pcc", "quectel_carrier_scc" WHERE $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "rat", "band" fill(none)
